status: 1.0.0 approved by Kevin on 2026-10-30 for the AIME run. 1.1.0 adds slugs that at least two analysis records asked for after synonyms were merged, for Kevin's review.
description: Controlled vocabulary for Kyuclid. status: observed = found in the 150-problem AIME taxonomy sample; seeded = expected from the task brief or later waves, not yet seen; seed-problem = used by the seed problems; pilot-proposed = asked for by the analysis passes on the pilot. run-proposed = asked for by at least two records of the full run. legacy = kept only so that seed problems validate, not for new tagging. sample_count counts sample problems.

techniques.definition: Treat nested absolute values as repeated reflections that fold a graph onto one fundamental piece.
Scale one axis to turn an ellipse into a circle, keeping ratios along parallel lines.
Use the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality to optimise a product under a fixed sum.
Compare arithmetic and harmonic means.
Use that an angle bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of adjacent sides.
Derive unknown angles from angle sums, parallels, isosceles triangles and circles.
Expand trigonometric functions of a sum of angles, notably tangent addition.
Find an area by partitioning a region or subtracting pieces from a known shape.
Relate a triangle's area, its sides and its circumradius.
Relate lengths and areas through triangles that share a height or base.
Sum an arithmetic progression using term count and mean of the endpoints.
Combine a linear mix of sine and cosine into a single shifted sinusoid.
Find an overall speed as total distance over total time.
Compute in barycentric coordinates relative to a reference triangle.
Reason about a number through its digits in a non-decimal base.
Count one set by matching it one-to-one with an easier set.
Simplify ratios of binomial coefficients to linear or rational expressions.
Use the probability of a given number of successes in independent trials.
Count unordered selections with binomial coefficients.
Expand a power of a sum, or recognise an expression as one.
Group the terms of a sum into blocks on which the summand is constant or repeats.
Use inequalities to restrict unknowns to a small range or to prove an extremal bound, then check candidates or exhibit an example attaining it.
Get the area of a cyclic quadrilateral from its sides through the semiperimeter product.
Count orbits by averaging the number of objects fixed by each symmetry.
Track how carries in an addition change digit sums or digit counts.
Split a count into exhaustive, disjoint cases and sum.
Count balanced sequences or constrained lattice paths with the reflection argument.
Pin down additive functions, using regularity conditions to force linearity.
Bound a linear expression by the product of the norms of two vectors.
Bisect an area with a line through a centre of symmetry of the pieces it cuts.
Sum squared distances from a point to a set as the count times the squared distance to the centroid, plus a constant.
Relate cevian ratios to concurrency.
Reject algebraic solutions using domain, convergence, sign or convexity constraints.
Use the Chevalley-Warning theorem to force a non-trivial zero over a finite field.
Find the angle between clock hands from their rates.
Treat a relation as a polynomial identity and equate coefficients to find unknown constants.
Read a sum of coefficients by evaluating a polynomial at a chosen value.
Colour a board or structure so that a parity or balance obstruction appears.
Count the complement of the desired set and subtract from the total.
Rewrite a quadratic expression as a square plus a constant to read off a centre or extremum.
Place points as complex numbers, often on the unit circle, and compute.
Interpret multiplication by a complex number as rotation and scaling, adding arguments.
Update a probability on an event, including Bayes-style reversals.
Use the constant focal sum or difference of a conic, or its reflection property.
Use that a complex number times its conjugate equals its squared modulus.
Use that non-real roots of a real polynomial occur in conjugate pairs.
Place the figure on coordinates and compute with equations of lines, curves or points.
Use coprimality to transfer divisibility from a product to one factor.
Count with a known multiplicity, then divide or subtract to remove duplicates.
List or count the residues coprime to a modulus.
Reduce a three-dimensional configuration to a well-chosen planar section.
Combine or count congruences modulo coprime moduli independently.
Decompose a structure uniquely into cycles and count by cycle-size partition.
Count permutations with no fixed point.
Relate the curvatures of four mutually tangent circles by a quadratic identity.
Bound the number of positive roots from sign changes in the coefficients.
Rewrite a difference of two squares as a product to simplify or factor.
Relate a digit sum to the residue of the number.
Realise a dihedral angle as a planar angle between perpendiculars to the common edge.
Use that the squared components of a unit vector along orthogonal directions sum to one.
Compute a point's distance from a line with the standard formula.
Use a digit-based divisibility criterion.
Count divisors from the exponents in a prime factorisation.
Pair each divisor with its cofactor about the square root.
Convert between trigonometric values at an angle and at its double or half.
Count one quantity in two ways and equate the results.
Analyse each ground element's status or contribution separately, then combine.
Find the curve touched by a family of lines or curves, as the limit of intersections of neighbouring members.
Separate a complex relation into its real and imaginary components.
Use repeated division to solve a linear equation with coprime coefficients.
Relate the numbers of vertices, edges and faces of a convex polyhedron.
Count or sum values coprime to an integer with the totient function.
Use degree parity to decide when a graph has a trail using every edge once.
Write a random count as a sum of indicators and add their expectations.
Consider a largest or smallest object and derive structure from its extremality.
Rewrite an equation as a product equal to a known integer and enumerate factor pairs.
Write a polynomial as a product over its roots to evaluate or compare it.
Reason about the size or divisibility of factorials.
Compute a probability as favourable equally likely outcomes over all outcomes.
Reduce exponents with Fermat little theorem or Euler totient theorem.
Minimise a sum of distances to the vertices of a triangle at the point seeing each side under equal angles, often by a rotation.
Use repeated differences of a sequence to identify it as a polynomial of known degree.
Find the points fixed by an iterated map by factoring the fixed-point condition of its iterates.
Convert floor or fractional-part conditions to interval inequalities and locate where the value jumps.
Follow how one choice forces the next along a chain or board until the structure is fixed or contradicted.
Use the largest non-representable value of a linear form with coprime coefficients.
Substitute chosen values or expressions into a functional equation to extract structure.
Shift the elements of a selection to remove a no-two-adjacent constraint.
Encode a count as coefficients of a polynomial and manipulate it algebraically.
Recognise algebraic expressions as lengths or regions and solve the system geometrically.
Compute a probability as a ratio of measures on a continuous sample space.
Apply finite or infinite geometric series formulas, including blocks of consecutive terms.
Count solutions by sketching piecewise graphs and counting crossings of monotone pieces.
Model a structure as a graph and use degrees, cycles or connectivity.
Build an extremal object by making the locally best choice at each position.
Count Hamiltonian cycles in a structured graph by classifying how they must cross between its parts.
Use cross-ratio and harmonic division, and their projections.
Use the harmonic mean of two or more quantities.
Lift a solution of a polynomial congruence from a prime power to a higher power of that prime.
Compute a triangle's area from side lengths via the semiperimeter.
Sum binomial coefficients along a diagonal of Pascal's triangle as one binomial coefficient.
Bound a product of sums with the generalised Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
Use a dilation that maps one figure to another, for tangent circles or parallel sides.
Correct for overlapping conditions by alternately adding and subtracting intersections.
Use a tangential polygon: equal tangent lengths from a point, and area equal to inradius times semiperimeter.
Use that an inscribed angle is half its arc and equal arcs give equal angles.
Split a solid into pyramids from the centre of its insphere, so that its volume is a third of the inradius times the surface area.
Find a quantity that a process leaves unchanged and compare start and end.
Use a function's inverse, involution property or fixed points to determine its form.
Invert about a circle to turn circles and tangencies into simpler objects.
Apply convexity to compare a function of a mean with the mean of the function.
Construct or evaluate the polynomial determined by its values at given points.
Count monotone grid paths with binomial coefficients or dynamic tables.
Relate three sides and one angle of a triangle.
Relate sides to the sines of opposite angles in a triangle.
Use a least common multiple or greatest common divisor to determine a smallest or largest value.
Find the exponent of a prime in a factorial by summing floors.
Add, subtract or multiply given equations, including all equations of a symmetric or cyclic system, to reach the target without solving fully.
Solve a linear equation in integers via divisibility and parametrisation.
Solve a constant-coefficient linear recurrence through its characteristic roots or a shift by its fixed point.
Set up and solve simultaneous linear equations.
Recognise the set of points meeting a metric condition as a standard curve, then compute with that curve.
Apply logarithm laws and change of base to reduce to algebraic relations.
Use lifting the exponent to find the power of a prime dividing a difference of powers.
Define states and solve linear equations for expected hitting times.
Assign weights to vertices to read off ratios along cevians.
Prove a formula or structural claim for all indices by induction.
Find a median's length from the sides, or the sides from the medians.
Relate ratios along a transversal to collinearity.
Compose fractional linear maps through their matrices or fixed points to read off an iterate.
Reduce a condition to congruences and work with residues.
Solve a linear congruence by multiplying by an inverse.
Use where a function increases or decreases to establish uniqueness, extrema or solution counts.
Find a quantity that changes in one direction, to prove termination or bound steps.
Use that an arithmetic function is multiplicative on coprime arguments.
Relate power sums of roots to the elementary symmetric functions.
Partition objects into orbits of a symmetry; a symmetric object is fixed by choosing one orbit representative.
Use the smallest exponent at which a power returns to one modulo something.
Relate an area to its projection by the scaling factor of the tilt.
Track the exponent of a prime in a factorial, binomial coefficient or product, including Legendre formula.
Pair terms of a sum so that each pair has a constant or simple value.
Divide a palindromic polynomial by a middle power and substitute the sum of the variable and its reciprocal.
Get the volume or surface of a solid of revolution from the path of the centroid of what is revolved.
Relate the squares of a parallelogram's diagonals to the squares of its sides.
Use parity to restrict the factors, terms or structure of a solution.
Split a rational function into simpler fractions, usually so that a sum telescopes or roots become visible.
Express entries of an additive triangular array as binomially weighted sums of the base row.
Solve a Pell-type equation through its fundamental solution.
Use that curves through prescribed points form a small linear family sharing further forced points.
Use that a perfect square has even prime exponents.
Use the periods of a sequence or of trigonometric functions to reduce an index or an angle condition.
Count arrangements of a multiset using multinomial coefficients.
Relate a lattice polygon area to its interior and boundary lattice points.
Force a coincidence because there are more objects than classes.
Express digits algebraically through powers of the base.
Find the equation of a plane through given points and intersect it with lines or edges.
Reflect a point through a midpoint to create a parallelogram or to bring separate segments together.
Write complex numbers in polar form so powers and products act on the argument.
Use the interior angle measure of a regular polygon as a function of its side count.
Factor an expression or polynomial by grouping or by finding a root, reducing its degree.
Build a new polynomial whose roots are a function of the original roots.
Equate products of secant or chord segments through a point with respect to a circle.
Reduce high powers of an algebraic number using the low-degree polynomial it satisfies.
Use closed forms for sums of squares or higher powers of consecutive integers.
Factor integers into primes and reason about the exponents.
Name the terms of an arithmetic or geometric progression with a few parameters and derive constraints.
Relate the sides and diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral.
Set up equations from right triangles using the Pythagorean theorem.
Use the sum of squares of sine and cosine to eliminate a variable.
Parametrise or list integer right triangles.
Use the sign or vanishing of a discriminant to bound a parameter or force a repeated root.
Use which residues are squares, including Legendre symbols.
Use the locus of equal power with respect to two circles, and radical centres.
Translate rates, times, or mixture proportions into equations.
Write a rational ratio in lowest terms and use integrality to force divisibility.
Restrict rational roots of an integer polynomial by the end coefficients.
Maximise or minimise a sum of products through the ordering of the factors.
Count or compute by a recurrence, table or tree built from smaller states, including rewriting or unrolling the recurrence.
Reflect points or curves across a line, using perpendicularity and the midpoint condition.
Count the regions cut by curves as a constant plus the curves plus their crossings.
Use that only the relative order matters and all orderings are equally likely.
Evaluate a polynomial at a root of a divisor to read off a remainder or factor.
Run a procedure backwards from its final state, where each step has few possible predecessors.
Express lengths in right triangles through tangent, sine or cosine of an angle.
Equate the path traced on a surface with the arc rolled out on the rolling body to relate rotation and travel.
Use the location and factorisation properties of roots of unity on the unit circle.
Average a generating polynomial over roots of unity to extract coefficients in a residue class.
Read a composition of two reflections in intersecting lines as a rotation by twice the angle between them.
Rotate part of a figure to create congruence or an equilateral triangle.
Multiply the numbers of independent choices made in sequence.
Describe a word by its maximal runs, so that adjacency conditions become conditions on the run lengths.
Use that a quantity varying linearly along a segment is a weighted average of endpoint values.
Multiply conditional probabilities through a sequence of stages.
Add a constant to a bilinear expression so it factors as a product of two shifted terms.
Compute a polygon area from its vertex coordinates.
Establish similar triangles and use proportional sides.
Compute a triangle's area from two sides and the sine of the included angle.
Shift or shrink a parametrised figure until it touches its container, so that an extreme case can be assumed.
Compute small cases, conjecture a general form, then confirm it.
Move variables closer together or to extremes while improving a quantity, to locate the optimum.
Recognise a solid as a piece of a simpler one by cutting it or joining copies.
Write an expression as a sum of squares to prove non-negativity or find equality.
Use the rotation-dilation taking one segment to another, and its centre.
Isolate radicals and square to obtain a polynomial equation.
Count multisets or non-negative integer solutions of a fixed sum with separators.
Find a cevian length from the sides and the division of the opposite side.
List representations of an integer as a sum of two squares.
Rewrite a symmetric expression in terms of the sum and product of its variables.
Use symmetry to fix an element, assume an ordering, or halve the cases.
Use a tangent line or tangent circles, perpendicular to the radius at the contact point.
Bound a function by its tangent line at the equality point, then sum.
Rewrite terms as differences so that a sum or product collapses.
Count tilings of a board by recursion on the last piece.
Use the triangle inequality as a condition or to force a degenerate or extremal case.
Prove concurrency, or find ratios, with the sine form of Ceva.
Replace an algebraic variable by a trigonometric function to expose an identity.
Convert between sums and products of sines and cosines.
Flatten a solid or reflect a path to turn a shortest route into a straight line.
Evaluate a sum of products of binomial coefficients as a single binomial coefficient.
Introduce a new variable to turn an expression into a simpler or lower-degree form.
Represent displacements or points as vectors and sum or cross them.
Relate a polynomial's coefficients to the symmetric functions of its roots.
Use the other root of a quadratic to descend from one integer solution to a smaller one.
Compute the volume of a pyramid or tetrahedron, choosing a convenient base.
Evaluate a sum of binomial coefficients weighted by their index.
Use the value of a factorial modulo a prime.
Use the existence of a primitive prime divisor of a power difference.

configurations.definition: An angle subtended by a diameter is a right angle.
The locus of points with a fixed ratio of distances to two points.
An internal angle bisector meets the circumcircle at the midpoint of the opposite arc, on the side's perpendicular bisector.
A point whose cyclic angles to the sides of a triangle are all equal.
Medians meeting at the centroid, which splits them in a fixed ratio and the area equally.
A row of equal tangent circles along a side or inside an angle, whose total length gives a linear relation with the radius.
The region between a chord and its arc, equal to a sector minus a triangle.
The meeting point of the tangents to a triangle's circumcircle at two vertices.
The sphere through all vertices of a pyramid, with its centre on the axis.
A line tangent to two circles, with radii to the tangency points parallel.
A line tangent to two circles on opposite sides, passing through their internal centre of similitude.
Four lines and their six intersection points, with their diagonals.
Concentric circles bounding annular regions, whose areas are differences of squares of radii.
Four concyclic points, giving supplementary opposite angles and equal subtended angles.
A pyramid with equal edges from the apex, whose altitude meets the base at its circumcentre.
A polygon with all angles equal, so that its sides are vectors with fixed turning angles.
The line through the circumcenter, centroid and orthocenter, with its fixed ratio.
A circle tangent to one side and the extensions of the other two, with its tangent lengths.
Points seeing a fixed segment under a constant angle lie on a circular arc.
A figure folded onto itself, with the crease as the perpendicular bisector of a point and its image.
A cyclic quadrilateral with equal products of opposite sides.
The points on a median or symmedian defined by circles through a vertex and tangent to a side.
The angle at an incenter subtending a side, a right angle plus half the opposite angle.
The midpoint of an arc is equidistant from two vertices, the incenter and the excenter.
A triangle or tangential polygon with its incircle, whose tangency points split sides into tangent lengths.
The incircles or incenters of the two subtriangles created by a segment from a vertex to the opposite side.
A quadrilateral with one vertex on each side of a rectangle, sharing the rectangle's centre.
A tetrahedron with congruent faces, inscribable in a rectangular box with edges as face diagonals.
An isosceles trapezoid, decomposed by altitudes from the shorter base.
An isosceles triangle whose apex altitude is also a median and an angle bisector.
The triangle of side midpoints, homothetic to the original.
The median to the hypotenuse equals half the hypotenuse, making the midpoint the circumcentre.
The common point of the four circumcircles of a complete quadrilateral.
A circle tangent to two sides of a triangle and internally to its circumcircle.
Circles tangent internally or externally, whose centres and tangency point are collinear.
A square inside another square, with congruent or similar right triangles in the corners.
The circle through the side midpoints, altitude feet and orthocenter-vertex midpoints.
The triangle of altitude feet, whose incenter is the orthocenter.
Reflections of the orthocenter in the sides and midpoints lie on the circumcircle.
Segments parallel to a triangle's side, including midlines, cutting similar triangles.
The perpendicular from a circle's centre bisects a chord and forms a right triangle with the radius.
A quadrilateral with an incircle, whose opposite sides have equal sums.
The polygon or curve in which a plane cuts a polyhedron or cylinder.
A regular polygon divided into isosceles triangles from its centre, with vertices on a circumcircle.
A regular tetrahedron, with a known volume and a square midsection between opposite edges.
Congruent rhombi around a central rhombus, sharing its sides.
The altitude to the hypotenuse creates similar triangles and geometric-mean relations.
The feet of perpendiculars from a point on the circumcircle are collinear.
Right triangles with standard acute angles and known side ratios.
A square inscribed in a right triangle, either at the right angle or on the hypotenuse.
A rectangle dissected into squares, whose sizes add along shared edges.
The reflection of a median in the angle bisector, and the tangent-intersection construction.
Spheres resting on or against a plane and tangent to each other or to a second plane, with centres at known heights.
A trapezoid whose legs are extended to meet, forming similar triangles.
A triangle specified by its altitudes, with sides inversely proportional to them.
A corner of a box where three mutually perpendicular edges meet, giving a pyramid cut from a cube.
Two circles meeting at two points, with a common chord or a line through an intersection point.
Two tangents to a circle from an external point, equal in length with the centre on the bisector.
